content: Hello! I'm hoping to get some help with PR #36506. After applying a reviewer's suggestion, I hit a style linter failure complaining about Windows line endings. In my attempt to fix it, an auto-formatting script seemingly ran and rewrote the entire file, and I'm currently unable to cleanly revert the unintended changes. I'd really appreciate some guidance on how to resolve this. Thanks!

I don't have concrete example in hand but there are a few tricks to resolve this

  • configure git to automatically store Windows ending in local file, and commit Unix ending to remote
  • use an editor that automatically detect the codebase ending and continue using it. I think vscode already does this?
Also, you can try using git reflog to find an good old version and revert to it

Weiyi Wang said:

I think vscode already does this?

VSCode only detects the current file's line endings. But since mathlib has ./.vscode/settings.json with "files.eol": "\n", if you open mathlib's root folder in vscode then it'll also work for new files you create.

When using Windows I recommend git config --global core.autocrlf false (and also "files.eol": "\n" in vscode), then if you already cloned mathlib- delete it and clone a fresh copy. That makes everything LF, and you never have to worry about CRLF.

Oh and also since you seemed to have pushed 2 CRLF files to your repo, after you reclone, open these two files in VSCode and on the bottom right click "CRLF", then switch the file to "LF", save and commit.

Thanks! The lint style check has passed and I'm just waiting on the rest CI now. I was unaware of the CRLF/LF conflict. Turns out my entire local mathlib was in CRLF. I've now turned off the auto-conversion and recloned a fresh copy, so all files are finally in LF.
I've also had this happen recently. You can also do: git add --renormalize ., but I think this is some sort of new GitHub bug.
Adding the mixed-line-ending hook to the pre-commit config would be a good idea here.
